classroom_steps.text: A load bends a spring away from its unloaded shape. The spring exerts a restoring force.
In an ideal elastic model, increasing deflection increases restoring force. A real component has a range over which that model is useful.
Material, geometry and manufacturing choices affect performance. Standen’s describes modelling and heat-treatment methods; the illustration is not its production specification.
Testing compares the component with its intended duty. A spring that remains deformed after unloading raises a different question from one that returns to its starting shape.

discussion: Would the stiffest possible spring always be the best suspension spring?
activity: Use an invented table: load 0, 100, 200, 300 N; deflection 0, 2, 4, 6 mm. Plot load against deflection, calculate the model stiffness, and predict 400 N only within the assumed elastic range. A second sample retains 1 mm deflection after unloading: discuss why the same model may no longer describe it.
teacher_note: The numbers are invented teaching data, not Standen’s test results. A leaf-spring assembly is not necessarily linear at every load. Spring stiffness, damping and material strength are different properties.

classroom_steps.text: Stored grain and associated organisms can remain biologically active. Temperature, moisture and ventilation influence conditions in storage.
Respiration releases energy and can produce CO2. OPI uses CO2 measurements as an indicator alongside temperature and moisture.
A measurement describes the air at a sensor and a moment in time. Airflow and placement affect what that reading can reveal.
A changing pattern can prompt inspection or a management decision. Several measurements together are more informative than treating one CO2 value as proof of a particular problem.

discussion: What else would you measure before deciding that a CO2 increase means spoilage?
